ch26.d.V: Potential difference $V$ across the wire; 0 means no field
ch26.d.T: Hotter ions vibrate more and scatter electrons more often (shorter mean free time $\tau$)
ch26.d.A: Cross-sectional area $A$ of the wire (height in the drawing)
ch26.goal.drift: Electrons in a field accelerate between collisions and get a random direction at each one; on average they move at a steady drift velocity $v_d$
ch26.goal.R: Scattering is the origin of resistance: $R = \rho L/A$, with resistivity $\rho$ proportional to the collision rate
ch26.obs.zero: Zero voltage: electrons move fast but in random directions, so the net charge through the cross-section stays at 0
ch26.obs.drift: With a voltage: the path of the outlined electron bends against $\vec E$ between collisions, and the whole population creeps to the left
ch26.obs.count: The slope of the net charge $Q(t)$ through the orange dashed cross-section is the current $I$; over a longer run $\bar I = Q/t$ settles on the prediction (dashed)
ch26.obs.ohm: Measure at several voltages: the points on the $I$-$V$ chart lie on a straight line through the origin (Ohm's law)
ch26.obs.LA: Double the length: $R$ doubles. Double the cross-section: $R$ halves. Lines of wires measured earlier stay in grey
ch26.obs.T: Higher temperature: more frequent collisions, smaller $v_d$, larger $R$
ch26.assume.speed: Drift speed is hugely exaggerated: in copper $v_d \sim 10^{-4}$ m/s while the electron (Fermi) speed is $\sim 10^{6}$ m/s
ch26.assume.model: Drude model: fixed speed and random direction after each collision, exponentially distributed free times (mean $\tau \propto 1/T$), 2D section, no electron-electron interaction
ch26.assume.units: Each drawn electron stands for many electrons. Its charge is set so that a 4 cm, 2 mm², 300 K wire has 10 Ω. The count uses 8 times as many electrons as are drawn, to cut the thermal noise; $\bar I$ is shown from 3 s on
